evidence_quotes.quote: Repeated and prolonged periods when piped water is unavailable were reported, as was unreliable infrastructure, inadequate service delivery, empty reservoirs and poor supply exacerbated by droughts.
The objectives were to develop local knowledge on health priorities in a rural province as part of a programme developing community evidence for policy and planning.
Participants overwhelmingly related lack of water to poor planning by water authorities, municipality and service providers asserting that these groups are out of touch with realities on the ground

PAR was adopted to understand and enable interfaces between communities and public authorities. As a first step, articulating needs and priorities among community stakeholders, there was unanimity that water provision can only be of benefit with taps in households.

We then held a series of consensus-building workshops to develop accounts of the problem and actions to address it using Photovoice to document lived realities. Thematic analysis of narrative and visual data was performed.
Repeated and prolonged periods without piped water were recorded as was widespread use of informal and unregulated sources, several of which were known to be contaminated

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water service access in rural Mpumalanga, South Africa, documenting prolonged piped-water outages, non-functional boreholes/reservoirs, reliance on municipal water tankers and surface water, and community demand for household taps.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Plain wording (yes): the paper examines participatory water governance, perceived municipal planning and accountability deficits, local corruption, and institutional communication channels linking communities to local government (ward committees, Indunas, Community Development Forums, elected councillors and Integrated Development Plans). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (no): South Africa's constitutional and statutory water framework (National Water Act, Water Services Act, municipal devolution, CMAs/WUAs) appears only as unanalysed macro-governance background in the introduction, while the empirical study develops a participatory action research (PAR) process for community priority-setting, planning and advocacy around general municipal service-delivery and infrastructure-maintenance failures rather than analysing a rule-type mechanism directly governing access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, formal discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative empirical data from an eight-workshop participatory action research (PAR) and Photovoice study with 16 participants in the water-nominating village (and 48 participants across three villages overall), analysed via inductive/deductive thematic analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative household water-access outcomes including repeated and prolonged piped-water unavailability, empty reservoirs, broken borehole pumps, reliance on intermittent municipal mobile tankers and contaminated river/well water, water-fetching time/safety burdens, and financial strain from buying water from tankers.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and sample (adult community stakeholders in rural villages of the Agincourt HDSS, n=16 in Village A for water, n=48 across three villages), the governance/participatory phenomena examined, qualitative access conditions/outcomes, and the PAR/Photovoice qualitative study design are clearly identifiable, though the exposure is not an eligible rule-type legal/administrative mechanism under Criterion 2.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (workshops were conducted in xiTsonga with some English, transcribed verbatim and translated into English by the authors).

study_design: Qualitative participatory action research (PAR) with Photovoice and thematic analysis
population_and_sample: Adult community stakeholders (aged 18+, 81% female in water group) in rural villages of the Agincourt Health and Socio-Demographic Surveillance System, Mpumalanga, South Africa; n=16 participants in Village A nominating water (and n=48 participants across Villages A, B and C in combined workshops); unit of analysis: village stakeholder group and household lived experience
exposure: Participatory water governance / community-authority planning interfaces and perceived municipal service-delivery, infrastructure-maintenance and accountability failures (no rule-type legal or administrative mechanism empirically analysed)
outcome: Household drinking-water availability and reliability (prolonged piped-water interruptions, reliance on municipal mobile tankers and contaminated informal/surface sources, collection burden and financial cost of buying water from tankers)
rationale: Full text matches metadata (Hove et al. 2019, BMJ Global Health). This qualitative participatory action research (PAR) and Photovoice study empirically documents rural household drinking-water shortages, piped-supply interruptions, and reliance on mobile tankers and surface water in Mpumalanga, South Africa (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5 and c6). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because it examines participatory water governance, municipal planning/accountability failures, and local institutional communication structures (ward committees, Community Development Forums, councillors). However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, it is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure): statutory and decentralisation frameworks are discussed only as macro-governance background in the introduction, while the empirical study focuses on eliciting community priorities regarding general service-delivery/maintenance failures and building participatory planning/advocacy interfaces rather than analysing a rule-type legal, regulatory or administrative mechanism directly governing service access.
